1058.title: Christ the King
1058.hook: the last Sunday of the church year: a king crowned with thorns
1058.howItsDone: Catholic and some Protestant churches keep Christ the King on the last Sunday before Advent, with readings about Christ's kingship and hymns that call him king, and some end the service with a procession.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Remembrance: poppies, silence, and swords beaten into plowshares, and your line was we will remember.

A soldier is twisting thorn branches into a ring, carefully, so it holds its shape. Around him, the rest of the band are laughing. They have found a scarlet robe. Someone has a reed for a scepter. The prisoner is already beaten and tired, and they are about to crown him. A whole coronation, staged as a joke, in a governor's hall in Jerusalem. On the last Sunday of the church year, before Advent starts the circle again, Catholic and some Protestant churches keep a feast for the man under those thorns: Christ the King.
screen: `A SOLDIER TWISTS A RING OF THORNS.`
`THE LAST SUNDAY OF THE CHURCH YEAR.`

segments.voice: Look at what the soldiers do. Matthew tells it, in the King James words: "And when they had platted a crown of thorns, they put it upon his head, and a reed in his right hand: and they bowed the knee before him, and mocked him, saying, Hail, King of the Jews!" Crown, scepter, robe, a bended knee, a royal greeting: every part of a real coronation, all meant as mockery. Christians say the joke was true, and the soldiers didn't know it. Then the sign. John says Pilate wrote a title and had it put on the cross: Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews. Meant as a charge; read by Christians as a proclamation. Earlier that same morning, Pilate had asked Jesus straight out whether he was a king. Jesus answered: "My kingdom is not of this world." Not that it isn't real, Christians say, but that it doesn't come from here, and doesn't run on the same rules. Its king doesn't send soldiers. He washes feet. In Mark, Jesus says he came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life. So this feast turns a crown upside down. Paul, writing to the church at Philippi, says Jesus took the form of a servant, went all the way down to death on a cross, and that God lifted him high, so "that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow." The soldiers bowed the knee to mock him. Paul says every knee should bow, this time in earnest. Same motion, opposite meaning.
screen: `MY KINGDOM IS NOT OF THIS WORLD.`

segments.voice: Picture the ring of thorns and the reed, then someone in your own life who served without a crown: a nurse on a night shift, a parent at a sink, a neighbor who shoveled your path. Slowly lower your head. If you pray, bow to Christ the King with Paul's words, at the name of Jesus every knee should bow; if you don't, let the bow be thanks for everyone who serves.
Servant king. The feast's name for a king crowned with thorns, who came not to be served but to serve, and whose kingdom is not of this world.
Your line: a different king. His crown was made of thorns. Day one thousand fifty-eight, done.

1059.title: Thanksgiving
1059.hook: in North America, a harvest thanks at the table
1059.howItsDone: Some Christian families in the United States and Canada say grace before the Thanksgiving meal, sometimes holding hands, and some churches hold a Thanksgiving service or gather food for neighbors in need.

segments.voice: Yesterday, servant king: a crown of thorns, and your line was a different king.

The ship has been driven by a storm for fourteen days. No sun, no stars. The cargo has gone over the side. The sailors have just been caught trying to slip away in the lifeboat. It's the dark before dawn, and nobody has eaten properly since the storm began. Then a prisoner, a tentmaker called Paul, takes a loaf and does something ordinary. He says grace. A strange place to begin a day about Thanksgiving, North America's harvest meal with thanks at the table. But that's where today starts.

In Acts, in the King James words, Paul urges them all to eat, and then "he took bread, and gave thanks to God in presence of them all: and when he had broken it, he began to eat." The storm isn't over; the ship hasn't reached land. He gives thanks in the middle, in front of terrified people, and then: "Then were they all of good cheer, and they also took some meat." One person's grace turned into everyone's breakfast. That grace has a pattern behind it. In Mark, with a hungry crowd in the wilderness, Jesus takes the loaves, gives thanks, breaks them, and gives them to his disciples to set before the people. In Luke, two friends at Emmaus only recognize the risen Jesus when he takes bread, blesses it and breaks it. More than once, the meal begins with thanks. A letter in Paul's name says: "For every creature of God is good, and nothing to be refused, if it be received with thanksgiving." Creature there means every created thing. The potatoes count. And to the church at Thessalonica, Paul wrote: "In every thing give thanks." Not for every thing, some readers point out. In every thing. In the storm, too. At a Thanksgiving table, grace changes from house to house: a psalm, "O give thanks unto the LORD; for he is good: for his mercy endureth for ever," a grandmother's grace, or just hands held for a moment. The shape is the ship's: stop, give thanks out loud, then eat together.
screen: `JESUS TOOK THE LOAVES AND GAVE THANKS.`

segments.voice: Think of your next meal, and of one thing in your life still unsettled, a storm still going; don't try to solve it, just let it be there. Then choose a few plain words of thanks to say before that meal anyway. If you pray, use a grace your family knows, or the psalm's line, O give thanks unto the LORD; for he is good; if not, just choose the words, and the breath you'll pause for.
Thanksgiving. In North America, a harvest meal with thanks at the table. In the Bible, giving thanks in every thing, even in a storm.
Your line: for all good gifts. Thanks can come before the storm is over. That's day one thousand fifty-nine.

1060.title: St Andrew (30 November)
1060.hook: the first called, the one who brought his brother, near the start of Advent
1060.tomorrow: Year three close: the story and the circle
1060.howItsDone: Churches that keep saints' days remember Andrew on the thirtieth of November, and in Scotland, where he is patron saint, the day is also kept as a national celebration.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Thanksgiving: Paul giving thanks in the storm, and your line was for all good gifts.

"What seek ye?" In John's Gospel, in the King James words, Jesus turns round and asks it of two men who have been walking behind him. Their teacher, John the Baptist, had just pointed at him and said, "Behold the Lamb of God!" So they followed. They don't have a clever answer. They ask where he's staying. He says, "Come and see." And they spend the rest of that day with him. John's Gospel names one of the two: Andrew. And the next thing Andrew does is go and look for his brother. The church keeps his day on the thirtieth of November, near the start of Advent.

Then, John says, "He first findeth his own brother Simon, and saith unto him, We have found the Messias, which is, being interpreted, the Christ. And he brought him to Jesus." First findeth. Before anything else, he gets his brother. Jesus is about to give that brother a new name: Cephas, a stone. We know him as Peter. And John calls Andrew simply Simon Peter's brother. In the Orthodox tradition he is the First-Called: in John's telling, he follows Jesus before Peter arrives. Watch what he keeps doing. A huge crowd on a hillside, nothing to eat, the disciples worried. It's Andrew who notices a boy: "There is a lad here, which hath five barley loaves, and two small fishes: but what are they among so many?" He doesn't solve the problem. He just brings the boy, and the little he has, to Jesus. Later, in Jerusalem, some Greeks come asking to see Jesus. They ask Philip. Philip tells Andrew, and Andrew and Philip go and tell Jesus. A brother, a boy, a group of strangers: each time, Andrew is bringing someone. There John's story of him ends. Tradition says he traveled far to preach and died on a cross shaped like an X, and that cross now sits on the flag of Scotland, where he's the patron saint. His day near the start of Advent fits him: the season of waiting opens with the man who said, we have found him, and went to get someone else.

Think of one good thing you've found, a walk, a choir, a quiet church, a book, a kitchen table where people are kind, and then of one person who might need it: not the easiest to ask, but the one who came to mind first. Picture yourself asking plainly, with the words Andrew first heard: come and see. If you pray, pray for that person by name; if you don't, just hold them in mind.
St Andrew. Simon Peter's brother, the one who kept bringing people to Jesus, remembered on the thirtieth of November.
Your line: we have found him. Andrew's first thought was his brother. Until tomorrow.

1061.title: Year three close: the story and the circle
1061.hook: a long line from Jericho to Lagos, and a year that keeps turning
1061.howItsDone: Western churches that follow the church year mark its turning at Advent (the Orthodox year begins on 1 September), and some end the old year with Christ the King and begin the new one with the first Advent candle, telling the same story again.

segments.voice: Yesterday, St Andrew, who found his brother, and your line was we have found him.

Twelve stones, piled up near Jericho. Each was carried on a man's shoulder from the dry riverbed where the priests stood, one man for each tribe. Joshua tells them the stones are for the children. That was near the start of this year: Israel crossing the Jordan. From there the story ran a long line, through judges and kings, exile and return, apostles and martyrs, monks and reformers, all the way to churches in Lagos. Then the line bent into a circle: the church's year of feasts, from Advent candles to a king crowned with thorns. Today, both close.

This year had two shapes. The first was a line: Israel's story from Joshua to the return from exile; the early church, its martyrs and its creeds; the middle centuries, east and west, cathedrals and crusades, mystics and plague; the reformations, Protestant and Catholic, with saints and failures on both sides; then the church spreading across the world, to Lagos and far beyond. A line has a direction. It says: this happened, then this, and it matters what came first. The second shape was a circle. These last weeks walked the church year: Advent and Christmas, Lent and Easter, Pentecost, saints' days, All Souls, Christ the King. A circle comes round again. In Western churches, the first Advent candle will soon be lit again. Ecclesiastes knew both shapes: "One generation passeth away, and another generation cometh: but the earth abideth for ever." The generations are the line. The earth and its seasons are the circle. Back to the stones by the Jordan. Joshua says they are a sign, so that "when your children ask their fathers in time to come, saying, What mean ye by these stones?" someone will tell them the story. That's how the line keeps going: a child asks, and someone answers. And that's why the circle matters: every year the feasts come round, and the story is told again. The psalm puts it in one breath: "One generation shall praise thy works to another." The line hasn't ended. The circle keeps turning. And somewhere on both, there's a spot marked today.

Let the year pass by, from the river stones to the churches in Lagos and the candles and feasts, and ask where you are in it today: inside it, beside it, at the door, still deciding; all of those are places. Find one honest sentence that says where you stand, and write it down. If you pray, you can offer that sentence to God; if you don't, just keep it.
Ecclesiastes. The Bible's book of the turning seasons, which knew both shapes this year walked: a line, and a circle.
Your line: the circle turns. Tomorrow, year four begins: many rooms, and how people talk about God. Year three, done.

1062.title: Talking about God
1062.hook: a kitchen-table question, a half answer, and a new year of many rooms
1062.howItsDone: Christians do theology in sermons, catechism classes, Bible studies and universities, and also at kitchen tables; Christian teachers have long paired careful words about God with an honest admission that God is beyond them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, year three closed: a line from Jericho to Lagos, and a circle of feasts. Your line was the circle turns. Where did you put your sentence? Day one thousand sixty-two.

A kid at the kitchen table, spoon halfway to her mouth, asks: where is God, exactly? Her dad opens his mouth to answer. Gets three words in. Stops. Starts again. That pause, between a real question and an honest answer, is where year four begins. It's called many rooms, after a line of Jesus in John's Gospel: "In my Father's house are many mansions." This year walks through the big questions one room at a time, and listens to how different churches answer them. The first question sits under all the others: can anyone talk about God at all? Today's word: theology.

Theology. The word is usually explained as words about God. It sounds like something for professors in libraries. But the kid's question is theology, and so is her dad's half answer. Anyone who has said God is good, or asked why God feels far away, has done some. And the Bible itself is careful about those words. In Isaiah, God says: "For my thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways my ways." Then a picture of the distance: "as the heavens are higher than the earth, so are my ways higher than your ways." Job and his friends talk about God for chapter after chapter. When God finally answers out of the whirlwind, Job says: "therefore have I uttered that I understood not; things too wonderful for me, which I knew not." Paul puts it in one line: "For now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face." A glass there is a mirror, and a dim one. So words fall short. And yet the same Bible keeps using them. Peter's letter tells Christians to "be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you." A reason. Words, offered out loud. Christian teachers have held both of those at once: no sentence can hold God, and sentences still help, the way a dad's three halting words still tell a kid that her question was a good one. That's the job of this year. Not to settle the big questions, but to hear how people have tried to answer them, carefully, and with their words a little short.

Here's the practice: write one sentence about God. Settle, and breathe. Let a sentence come. What you believe, what you doubt, what you were taught, what you wish were true. I don't know is a sentence too. Don't polish it. When the bell ends, write it down and look at it. Notice where it reaches, and where it runs out. If you pray, you can hold that sentence up just as it is. The bell holds the time.
Theology. Words about God: never quite enough, and still worth saying.
Your line: words fall short, and help. Keep your sentence somewhere you'll find it again this year, and see whether it changes. Day one thousand sixty-two.

1063.title: Where authority comes from
1063.hook: Protestants say scripture alone is the final authority; Catholics and Orthodox read scripture within the church's living tradition
1063.howItsDone: Protestant churches teach that scripture is the final authority, often while still saying the ancient creeds; Catholic and Orthodox churches read scripture together with the church's tradition, councils and teachers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, theology: words about God. Your line was words fall short, and help. What was the one sentence you wrote? Day one thousand sixty-three.

Paul and Silas slip out of one Greek city by night and arrive in a town called Berea. They go to the synagogue and Paul speaks. The listeners don't simply nod along, and they don't throw him out either. They open the scriptures, and keep checking, day after day, whether what he said holds up. The book of Acts admires them for it: "These were more noble than those in Thessalonica." Which raises a question that would one day divide churches. When a teacher and a text seem to disagree, who has the final word? Today's word: sola scriptura.

Sola scriptura is Latin for scripture alone. It became a watchword of the Protestant Reformation. Luther and other Reformers said the Bible is the final authority, over every teacher, council and pope. Tradition can be good and useful, they said, but scripture is the judge of it. And they pointed to Berea: the people there "searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so," even with an apostle in the room. Catholics and Orthodox Christians see it another way. For them, scripture and the church's living tradition belong together. The New Testament was written inside the church, and the whole Bible was read aloud in its worship and handed on with its teaching, so it is read within that tradition, not apart from it. Catholics speak of the church's teaching office guarding the faith; the Orthodox speak of the councils, the early fathers and the mind of the church. They point to Paul: "stand fast, and hold the traditions which ye have been taught, whether by word, or our epistle." By word, or by letter. Both. And each side has its reply. Protestants say the apostles' teaching is now found in their writings, so scripture is where you check it. Catholics and Orthodox ask who decides what scripture means when sincere readers disagree. Protestants add that scripture alone was never meant to be scripture with no history: Lutheran and Anglican churches, among others, still say the old creeds, because they hold that the creeds agree with the Bible. Underneath the argument is a question that turns up in ordinary life too. When good voices disagree, whose do you trust, and why?

Here's the practice: notice who you trust, and why. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one question that matters to you. What's right, what's true, what to do next. Now notice where you go first for an answer. A book. A pastor. A parent. A friend. Your own gut. Just notice it, without grading it. Then ask, gently, why that voice. Because it has been right before? Because it loves you? Because it was simply there first? If you pray, you can bring the question to God as well. The bell holds the time.
Sola scriptura. Latin for scripture alone: the Protestant teaching that the Bible is the final authority over every other voice.
Your line: where do you stand? Today, when someone tells you something is true, notice for a second what you check it against. Day one thousand sixty-three.

1064.title: Four sides
1064.hook: Methodists speak of scripture, tradition, reason and experience working together
1064.howItsDone: Methodist churches teach that scripture is the primary source of faith, read with the help of tradition, reason and experience, and some study groups think a question through by asking what each of the four sides says.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sola scriptura: scripture alone, and the Bereans checking an apostle against the text. Your line was where do you stand? Whose voice did you notice yourself trusting first? Day one thousand sixty-four.

A rider on a country road in England, saddlebags heavy with books, heading for the next village to preach in a field. That's how John Wesley is remembered: an Anglican priest whose followers became the Methodists. Tradition says he read on horseback. He argued with friends by letter. And when a hard question came up, he didn't reach for just one thing. Methodists still speak of the habit he left them: four things, working together, when you think a question of faith through. Today's word is the shape of that habit: four sides.

The four sides are scripture, tradition, reason and experience. Scripture comes first. The psalm says: "Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path." A lamp shows the next step, and Methodists start there. Then tradition: what the church has said and prayed before you arrived. Jeremiah has the line: "ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein." The creeds, the old teachers, the hymns, are a kind of old path. Then reason. In Isaiah, God says: "Come now, and let us reason together." Thinking carefully isn't the enemy of faith in this picture. It's part of it. And last, experience. Wesley wrote in his journal about an evening meeting in London when, as he put it, his heart was strangely warmed, and he felt sure he was forgiven. Paul says something close to it: "The Spirit itself beareth witness with our spirit, that we are the children of God." A witness from the inside. Now the careful part. Methodist teachers say the four sides are not equal votes. Scripture is the ground. Tradition, reason and experience help you read it, test your reading, and live it. The name for the pattern came from later teachers looking back at how Wesley worked. And the sides check each other. A warm feeling that contradicts scripture gets questioned. A reading of scripture that no one in the church has ever held gets a second look. A neat argument that crushes real people's lives gets tested against what has actually happened to them.

Here's the practice: check one belief against all four sides. Settle, and breathe. Pick one thing you hold to be true about God, or about how to live. Small is fine. Now walk around it slowly. What does scripture say, as far as you know? What has the church said before? Does it make sense when you think it through? And how has it gone in your own life? You won't finish in two minutes. Just notice which side feels solid, and which side you've never checked. If you pray, you can ask for light on that side. The bell holds the time.
Four sides. Scripture, tradition, reason and experience: the Methodist way of turning a question of faith all the way round, with scripture as the ground.

Your line: four sides of a question. This week a year closed and the first rooms opened: words about God, who has the final word, and now four sides. Today, look at one question from a side you usually skip. Day one thousand sixty-four.
